title: Understanding and Defending VLM Jailbreaks via Jailbreak-Related Representation Shift
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Prior work assumes failures stem from models not recognizing harmful inputs; ours shows they recognize harm yet fail to act on it.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels, left old vs right new, example above embedding space
description: The figure is split by a dashed vertical line into two panels. The left, under a gray header reading 'Old hypothesis: Safety perception failure', and the right, under a blue header reading 'New hypothesis: Recognize-but-fail-to-refuse (Ours)'. Each panel stacks chat examples on the left and a blob-shaped VLM representation space on the right. Chat examples pair a hacker icon with a speech bubble query and a robot reply, with a screenshot image beside the multimodal query. In the old panel, benign (blue) and jailbreak (red) dots overlap in one region below a green harmful-refusal cluster. In the new panel, the space is cleanly divided into three colored regions: red jailbreak, green refusal and blue benign. Dashed arrows link replies to points. Captions at the bottom highlight ambiguity versus safety warnings.
caption: Comparison of two VLM jailbreak hypotheses. The safety perception failure hypothesis assumes that VLMs struggle to distinguish between benign and harmful inputs, based on implicitly harmful data with semantic and causal ambiguities. In contrast, our recognize-but-fail-to-refuse hypothesis posits that VLMs recognize harmful intent but fail to refuse. This hypothesis is grounded in explicitly harmful data and supported by the observations that (1) jailbreak responses often contain safety warnings, and (2) benign, refusal, and jailbreak samples are separable in representation space.
abstract: Large vision-language models (VLMs) often exhibit weakened safety alignment with the integration of the visual modality. Even when text prompts contain explicit harmful intent, adding an image can substantially increase jailbreak success rates. In this paper, we observe that VLMs can clearly distinguish benign inputs from harmful ones in their representation space. Moreover, even among harmful inputs, jailbreak samples form a distinct internal state that is separable from refusal samples. These observations suggest that jailbreaks do not arise from a failure to recognize harmful intent. Instead, the visual modality shifts representations toward a specific jailbreak state, thereby leading to a failure to trigger refusal. To quantify this transition, we identify a jailbreak direction and define the jailbreak-related shift as the component of the image-induced representation shift along this direction. Our analysis shows that the jailbreak-related shift reliably characterizes jailbreak behavior, providing a unified explanation for diverse jailbreak scenarios. Finally, we propose a defense method that enhances VLM safety by removing the jailbreak-related shift (JRS-Rem) at inference time. Experiments show that JRS-Rem provides strong defense across multiple scenarios while preserving performance on benign tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/LeeQueue513/JRS-Rem.
